name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,447

clue.text: Spirit shown by bishop in the mood for it

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
randy means feeling amorous, in the mood for sex

explanation.surface: A clergyman's lively spirits seem to have got him in the mood for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' tempts you toward a holy or ghostly sense beside a bishop, but it is the drink. 'In the mood for it' is British slang for feeling frisky: randy.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandy is a distilled alcoholic drink, and distilled liquors are generically called spirits.

clue.text: Support taking depressed chicken out?

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
feeling down is feeling depressed

explanation.surface: Someone offers help to a gloomy friend who has lost their nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' looks like a bird on a plate, but 'chicken out' is the phrasal verb for losing courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe withdrawing from a confrontation or commitment through lack of nerve.

clue.text: Line of male descent corrupted - not again!

indicators.note: something corrupted has been altered from its proper form, so the letters of 'not again' are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A weary exclamation at yet another scandal in a family's paternal line.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'not again!' reads as exasperation, and it is simply the eight letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnation is a technical term for kinship traced solely through fathers and sons.

clue.text: Free up time, having yen to get X-rated

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the word for 'free' runs backwards
having means holding on to as well, so the yen is attached to what comes before

blocks.note: to rid is to free
T is the standard abbreviation for time
Y is the symbol for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: Someone clears their diary, longing to watch something adult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free up time' reads as a single phrase about a diary; split it, and 'up' turns the synonym for free upside down in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Films rated X were explicit and indecent, and obscene material is commonly called filthy or smutty.

clue.text: Got a partner changing diaper? Winning!

indicators.note: changing a nappy is the surface, but changing the letters of 'diaper' rearranges them

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
a team that is winning is up, ahead in the score

explanation.surface: A new parent celebrates having someone to share nappy duty with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diaper' is the American word for a nappy, and changing one is the surface; here it is the letters that change.
explanation.definitionFit: To pair up is to join with someone else as a couple or team, so gaining a companion.

clue.text: Southern area with ultras all over the place

indicators.note: things all over the place are scattered in disorder, so the letters of 'ultras' are in a jumble

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for area
anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A part of the south overrun by rowdy hardline football fans.
explanation.walkthrough: Ultras are the most fanatical football supporters, which suits the rowdy surface; here they are just six letters to scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: Austral comes from the Latin word for the south wind and describes the southern hemisphere.

clue.text: Swimmer embarrassed (singular shrunken nut)

indicators.note: something shrunken has been made shorter, so the nut loses its final letter

blocks.note: embarrassed people go red in the face
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
an almond with its last letter cut off

explanation.surface: A swimmer is mortified by an unfortunate case of cold-water shrinkage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' suggests a person at the pool, and the aside about shrinkage keeps you there; in crosswords a swimmer is very often a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The sockeye, also called red salmon, is a fish of the North Pacific, and fish are creatures that swim.

clue.text: Girl that's after revolutionary British futon?

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so 'British futon' is flipped end to end
the phrase meaning 'that's' is placed behind, following what the rest of the clue builds

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British
a futon is a kind of bed
i.e. is short for id est, Latin for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A young woman is keen to get her hands on a radical piece of British furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as an adjective praising the futon's design; it reverses the British bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Debbie is a common female first name, and crosswords routinely define a given name by gender like this.

clue.text: A bit much to be hugged by a pool player?

indicators.note: being hugged means being wrapped in someone's arms, so 'a bit much' is held inside 'a'

blocks.note: 'a' as in 'ten pounds a head' means per
OTT stands for over the top, excessive

explanation.surface: Being embraced by a fellow at the pool table is a little excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'A' looks like an article, but it means per. The question mark flags a coined meaning: someone who pots balls at pool.
explanation.definitionFit: In pool and snooker the aim is to sink balls into pockets, called potting, so a player does exactly that.

clue.text: Cost to bury northern singer (deceased)

indicators.note: to bury something is to put it inside, so 'cost' encloses 'northern'

blocks.note: the price is what something costs
N is the standard abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: The expense of a funeral for a late singer from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: The burial in the surface fits the deceased singer, which makes 'bury' feel like scene-setting rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince was the American pop star behind Purple Rain, who died in 2016.

clue.text: Colleagues criminal releases without right

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so 'releases' sits around 'right'

blocks.note: a con is a convict, a criminal
to release is to free
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A crook's accomplices are set loose without justice being done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' naturally reads as 'lacking', which would take an R away; here it means outside, so the R goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Confrères, borrowed from French for brothers, are fellow members of a profession or association.

clue.text: TV drama's earliest part reviewed as such?

definitions.text: TV drama's earliest part reviewed as such?

indicators.note: the earliest part of a word is where it begins, its opening letter
to review is to look back over, so the pieces are read backwards

blocks.note: the tube is slang for television
the opening letter of drama

explanation.surface: A critic writes up the first episode of a new television drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a first episode is a show's first appearance, and 'as such?' flags that the clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A first episode is a programme's initial showing before the public, which is exactly a first appearance or launch.

clue.text: Simple song Dutch cat cut originally

indicators.note: cutting something at its origin removes the start, so the cat loses its opening letter

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for Dutch
KITTY, a pet name for a cat, without its first letter

explanation.surface: A little tune sung in Dutch about a cat that has been trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Originally' can mean 'first letter kept'; here it modifies 'cut', so the first letter is the one to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A ditty is a short, light, uncomplicated tune or piece of verse.

clue.text: A pair of reports going into local story

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so the first part sits inside 'local'

blocks.note: used as it stands
the word 'reports' contains exactly two copies of one letter, its first and fifth
a local is a native of the place

explanation.surface: Two news items are worked into a tale about the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pair of reports' sounds like two news items, and it is literal: the two Rs you can see in the word 'reports'.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is an account of connected events, which is what a tale or story is.

clue.text: Sex? Hell yeah!

blocks.note: a coy idiom, 'making ...', stands for lovemaking
an exclamation of wild delight and enthusiasm

explanation.walkthrough: The question and its answer read as a single exchange, but each half is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a jokey noun for lovemaking in the phrase 'make whoopee' and a cry of excited celebration.

clue.text: Terrible options heartless unit identifies

indicators.note: terrible things are in a bad state, so the letters of 'options' are wrecked into a new order
without a heart means missing the middle, so the core letters of 'unit' are removed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
unit with its two middle letters taken away

explanation.surface: A cold, uncaring department names the poor choices available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless unit' sounds like an unfeeling squad, but it just loses its centre. The seven jumbled letters give the first word plus the O that starts the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To point something out is to draw attention to it, singling it out so others recognise it.

clue.text: Unlimited gin punches left Hoskins green

indicators.note: without limits means with its boundaries gone, so only the inside of 'gin' is kept
a punch drives into something, so the spirit goes between 'left' and 'Hoskins'

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
gin with its first and last letters gone
Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, who refers to himself

explanation.surface: Endless gin has knocked the setter sideways and left him looking queasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters name themselves in the clue to mean ME. 'Green' looks like the queasy colour of a heavy drinker, and it is the colour itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Lime is a bright yellowish shade named after the citrus fruit's skin.

clue.text: Grass-skirted femme fatale given a makeover

indicators.note: to skirt is to run around the edge, so 'grass' goes around the femme fatale

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass
a vamp is a seductive, dangerous woman

explanation.surface: A seductress in a Hawaiian grass skirt has had her look updated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass-skirted' reads as one hyphenated costume word; split, it is the grass doing the skirting.
explanation.definitionFit: To revamp something is to renovate or overhaul its appearance, giving it a fresh new look.

clue.text: Swimmer heading for airboat in Kent bay?

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, so only the start of 'airboat' is used
the letter from 'airboat' is placed inside the phrase 'Kent bay'

blocks.note: Kent, the English county, lies in the South East
the first letter of airboat
a bay is a reddish-brown horse

explanation.surface: A swimmer makes for a flat-bottomed boat in a bay on the Kent coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay' looks like a stretch of coast, and it is a brown horse. Kent is a county in south-east England, abbreviated SE.
explanation.definitionFit: The seahorse is a small upright fish, and crosswords often call any sea creature a swimmer.

clue.text: Fell sick with Scotch finally going to head

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the preceding word, its last letter
going to the head means moving to the front, so the selected letter comes first

blocks.note: the last letter of Scotch
to be sick is to be ill

explanation.surface: A drinker collapsed ill after the whisky went to their head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like the past tense of fall; it is a noun, the northern English word for an upland or mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Lake District and northern England a fell is a hill or stretch of high moorland.

clue.text: Lager lass and editor upended into coffee

indicators.note: upended means turned upside down, which in a down clue flips the editor
the flipped editor is put inside the coffee

blocks.note: ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
a latte is milky coffee

explanation.surface: A beer-drinking young woman and her editor, dunked into a coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladette is British slang for a young woman who drinks and behaves as boisterously as the lads; lager is her stereotypical drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The term arose in 1990s Britain for rowdy, pint-swilling young women copying laddish culture.

clue.text: Genuine (because wine almost finished)

indicators.note: almost finished means stopping just short of the end, so the wine loses its last letter

blocks.note: 'since' can mean because, as in 'since you ask'
RED, a wine, without its final letter

explanation.surface: An honest excuse offered in brackets: the bottle is nearly empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost finished' reads as the bottle running low, and it tells you to drop the wine's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sincere means what they say, free of pretence or deceit, so honest and real.

clue.text: Swine dwelling on The French fashions

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another is placed above it, so the dwelling comes first

blocks.note: a sty is where pigs are kept
les is French for 'the' before a plural noun

explanation.surface: A dig at French fashions as fit only for a pigsty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swine' could be a term of abuse aimed at the French; it is the pig whose home is a sty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fashions and styles are both the prevailing modes of dress or design at a given time.

clue.text: You might say yours truly is a dog

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the person, standing in for the noun

blocks.note: the person composing the puzzle refers to themselves as 'yours truly'
a breed of gundog, such as the Irish or English breed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yours truly' is the compiler speaking, so the first half is whoever wrote this clue. 'You might say' warns the phrase is a roundabout description.
explanation.definitionFit: The compiler of a crossword is its setter, and setters are also gundog breeds trained to point at game.

clue.text: Pilgrim papal mercifulness has saved

indicators.note: something saved is kept safe inside, so the phrase before holds the answer within it

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A pilgrim is rescued by the pope's clemency.
explanation.walkthrough: The religious surface keeps 'papal' and 'pilgrim' together; the answer straddles 'papal' and 'mercifulness'.
explanation.definitionFit: A palmer was a medieval pilgrim who brought back a palm frond as proof of visiting the Holy Land.

clue.text: Telex lady sent off in a dignified way

indicators.note: something sent off is dispatched and disrupted, so 'telex lady' is scrambled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: The woman on the telex machine dispatches a message with great decorum.
explanation.walkthrough: Telex was the teleprinter network businesses used before fax and email; the whole phrase is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Exalted means lofty or of high rank, so behaving with noble, elevated bearing and stateliness.

clue.text: Briefly show yourself to be ostentatious

blocks.note: to expose yourself for a moment, as an indecent exposer does
British slang for showy and vulgar, as a car or suit can be

explanation.surface: Advice on how to appear showy: make a brief appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half has a naughty second sense: the flasher who exposes himself for an instant.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means expose briefly; the British adjective means gaudy, showy and meant to impress.

clue.text: Having gone over time, run off quick

indicators.note: in a down clue going over something means sitting above it, so the running away comes before the time

blocks.note: to flee is to run away
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A worker who has overrun their hours dashes off in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having gone over time' reads as overrunning; in this down clue it tells you the escape sits above the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective is a literary word for swift or nimble, as in 'fleet of foot'.

clue.text: It seems plod regularly takes speed

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the phrase is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A dig at the police: apparently the local bobbies now take drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Plod is British slang for the police (after Mr Plod in Noddy), and speed is an amphetamine, which drives the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the pace or rate of movement, especially in music, so it means the rate of motion.

clue.text: New pear tree sliced by hard scytheman

indicators.note: a new version is a remade one, so the letters of 'pear tree' are rebuilt
a slice cuts into something, so 'hard' is inserted into the rearranged letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A young fruit tree gets cut down by a tough man wielding a blade.
explanation.walkthrough: The orchard surface is apt, since a man with a scythe does cut things down; here the grim figure of death is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grim Reaper, the personification of death, is traditionally pictured carrying a long curved blade for harvesting.

clue.text: Is a trier mixed up in unusual things?

indicators.note: mixed up means confused and out of order, so the letters of 'is a trier' are shuffled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone who keeps trying gets entangled in odd matters.
explanation.walkthrough: A trier is someone who keeps making an effort; the phrase is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarities are items seldom found or encountered, so they are out of the ordinary.

clue.text: Slice of spotted dick unfinished? It's filling stuff!

indicators.note: a slice is a small cut from the front, just the opening letter of 'spotted'
something unfinished lacks its end, so the slang word loses its final letter

blocks.note: the first letter of spotted
TODGER, British slang for penis, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A helping of half-eaten spotted dick, the classic British suet pudding, is praised as heavy food.
explanation.walkthrough: Spotted dick is a British steamed suet pudding with currants, and the obvious unit, but 'spotted' and 'dick' are split. Todger is cheeky British slang for penis.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodge is heavy, starchy food such as suet puddings that fills you up quickly.
